name: Science and nature - very easy (AI-written, not yet reviewed)
description: 17 very easy questions on science and nature, written by Claude on 2026-10-06 as the gentlest level of the 'Science and nature' review pack: things almost everyone knows, in one short plain sentence, worded for adults. They are marked easy with a note "very easy" until the very easy level lands. The independent fact-check kept 17 of 17 written, fixed 2 and deleted 0. Every question and answer needs checking by a person before anybody plays it.

source.name: Written by hand by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) on 2026-10-06, from its own knowledge plus the pages each item cites: no API call. 17 items cite a page the writing pass fetched on 2026-10-06 and quote the phrase on it that supports the fact; none rests on common knowledge. Then fact-checked item by item by a separate Claude pass on 2026-10-06 that did not write them (every cited page re-fetched and read for the fact, every answer, wrong answer, explanation and level checked; `checked` keeps who checked it and what was fixed; items that could not be made right, and duplicates of other packs, were deleted). Very easy items are marked difficulty "easy" with "note": "very easy" until the very easy level lands. A person still reviews it by playing.

review.how: Check every question, answer and explanation. Fix or delete what is wrong, set status to 'reviewed' with your name and the date, then move the file to packs/ and list it in pack_library.js.

items.question: What is wind?
items.explain: Wind powers sailing ships across the oceans.

source.title: Wikipedia: Wind
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Natural movement of air' and 'Wind powers the voyages of sailing ships across Earth's oceans'.

items.question: What color are most tree leaves in summer?
items.explain: Leaves are green because of a substance that soaks up light from the Sun.

source.title: Wikipedia: Leaf
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Leaves are mostly green in color due to the presence of a compound called chlorophyll' and 'absorbs light energy from the Sun'.

items.question: What is the loud rumble you hear after a flash of lightning?
items.explain: You see lightning first because light travels much faster than sound.

source.title: Wikipedia: Thunder
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Sound caused by lightning' and 'the lightning is seen before the thunder is heard'.

items.question: What does a thermometer measure?
items.explain: Many older thermometers used a thin line of mercury inside glass.

source.title: Wikipedia: Thermometer
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the fact-check pass; the page text contains: 'A thermometer is a device that measures temperature (the hotness or coldness of an object)' and 'Mercury thermometer (mercury-in-glass thermometer)'.

checked.fixed: explain no longer just restated the question; now adds the mercury-in-glass fact (page-supported)

items.question: Which of these will a magnet pick up?
items.explain: Magnets pull on metals such as iron and steel.

source.title: Wikipedia: Magnet
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'a force that pulls on other ferromagnetic materials , such as iron , steel'.

items.question: What does water turn into when it boils?
items.explain: Steam is water that has turned into vapor.

source.title: Wikipedia: Steam
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Steam is water vapor' and 'by boiling'.

items.question: What do we call it when ice turns into water?
items.explain: Scientists also call melting by another name, fusion.

source.title: Wikipedia: Melting
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Melting , or fusion , is a physical process that results in the phase transition of a substance from a solid to a liquid' and 'Melting ice cubes'.

items.question: Which of these floats on water?
items.explain: Cork comes from the bark of the cork oak tree.

source.title: Wikipedia: Cork (material)
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Cork is an impermeable buoyant material' and 'Quercus suber (the cork oak)'.

items.question: What do we call a sound that bounces back to you, like a shout in a canyon?
items.explain: Hard surfaces such as walls and mountains bounce sound waves back.

source.title: Wikipedia: Echo
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'an echo is a reflection of sound' and 'Walls or other hard surfaces, such as mountains and privacy fences, reflect acoustic waves'.

items.question: Clouds are made mostly of tiny drops of what?
items.explain: Some clouds are made of tiny ice crystals instead.

source.title: Wikipedia: Cloud
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'miniature liquid droplets , ice crystals' and 'Water , primarily, comprises the droplets'.

items.question: Which of these holds salty water?
items.explain: Each liter of seawater holds about 35 grams of dissolved salt.

source.title: Wikipedia: Seawater
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'seawater in the world's oceans has a salinity of about 3.5%' and 'approximately 35 grams'.

items.question: What do we call balls of ice that fall from storm clouds?
items.explain: Each ball of hail is called a hailstone.

source.title: Wikipedia: Hail
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'It consists of balls or irregular lumps of ice, each of which is called a hailstone'.

items.question: What do we call the line where the sky seems to meet the land or sea?
items.explain: For someone standing at the water's edge, the horizon is only about 3 miles away.

source.title: Wikipedia: Horizon
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the fact-check pass; the page text contains: 'Apparent curve that separates earth from sky' and 'for an observer with eye level above sea level by 1.8 metres (6 ft) , the horizon is at a distance of about 4.8 kilometres (3 mi)'.

checked.fixed: explain reworded ('a grown-up' -> 'someone standing at the water's edge'); note quotes the eye-height condition

items.question: Which tool makes tiny things look bigger?
items.explain: A magnifying glass uses a curved lens to enlarge what you see.

source.title: Wikipedia: Magnifying glass
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'A magnifying glass is a convex lens' and 'used to produce a magnified image of an object'.

items.question: On a sunny day, what dark shape follows you along the ground?
items.explain: A shadow forms where your body blocks the sunlight.

source.title: Wikipedia: Shadow
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Area where light is blocked by an object'.

items.question: What do we call the wet drops found on grass in the early morning?
items.explain: Dew forms as cool surfaces collect moisture from the air.

source.title: Wikipedia: Dew
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Droplets of water that form in the morning or evening' and 'As the exposed surface cools by radiating its heat, atmospheric moisture condenses'.

items.question: What do we call a large stream of fresh water flowing toward the sea?
items.explain: Some rivers flow into lakes or into other rivers instead.

source.title: Wikipedia: River
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'A river is a natural stream of fresh water' and 'such as an ocean , lake , or another river'.
